name: Sicilian Kan Variation
summary: The Kan (5...a6 with ...e6) is a flexible Open Sicilian that delays committing the knights and keeps hedgehog options.
intro: The Kan Variation, sometimes grouped with the Paulsen, arises after 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6. Black combines an early ...e6 with the useful rook-pawn move ...a6, delaying the development of the knights and keeping the pawn structure supremely flexible. It is prized for its resilience and for the many set-ups Black can adopt, from a Scheveningen-style ...d6 to a full hedgehog, while White must decide whether to grab space with the Maroczy Bind.
line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Kan is built on flexibility. By playing ...e6 and ...a6 before committing the knights, Black controls the b5-square, prepares queenside expansion with ...b5, and keeps the option of developing the king's knight to f6 or e7 depending on White's set-up. The pawn on a6 also supports the light-squared bishop's development to b7, from where it eyes e4 and the long diagonal. This restraint means Black rarely walks into a forced theoretical duel and instead reaches middlegames dictated by understanding.

A central strategic question is the placement of Black's dark-squared bishop and central pawns. Black can aim for a small, solid ...d6 structure in the spirit of the Scheveningen, or fianchetto and adopt a hedgehog with pawns on a6, b6, d6 and e6, coiled to strike with ...b5 or ...d5. White, for his part, must weigh the trade-off between the space-gaining Maroczy Bind with c4 and a freer piece game with Bd3, in which the bishop pressures the kingside but the c4-square is left available to Black's pieces.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: One of White's most principled tries is 5.c4, the Maroczy Bind, clamping down on the d5- and b5-squares and gaining a durable space advantage. Black responds by manoeuvring patiently, often with ...Nf6, ...Bb4 or ...Be7, ...d6 and a hedgehog set-up, waiting for the moment to break with ...b5 or ...d5. Handling the bind well requires precise piece placement, since Black's position is cramped but very hard to break down and rich in latent energy.

The other main approach is 5.Bd3, developing actively and preparing 0-0, c4 or Nc3 while training the bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal. After 5...Bc5, hitting the d4-knight, or 5...Nf6, the game usually transposes into flexible middlegames where White enjoys a lead in development and Black relies on solidity and counterpunching. White may also simply play 5.Nc3, keeping options open and often steering towards Scheveningen or Taimanov-style structures, against which Black continues with ...b5 and harmonious development.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The variation is named after the Estonian master Ilya Kan, who helped develop the ...a6 treatment of the ...e6 Sicilian in the early twentieth century, and it is closely related to the broader Paulsen complex named after the nineteenth-century master Louis Paulsen. Its blend of soundness and flexibility has made it a favourite of players seeking a reliable, low-risk Sicilian that still offers winning chances. It has been employed at the highest level as a practical weapon precisely because it minimises forced theory while retaining the Sicilian's characteristic counterattacking potential.
